A wrongdoer was given the chance to offer compensation and satisfy the injured party, and the vocabulary for that process is the root behind the verb at the end of this ayah. Everyone listening knew the sequence: accusation, then the offer to make good, then judgement. What the ayah describes is the middle step being removed.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb about being asked to make amends appears three times in the Quran, and in all three it is negated, so the Book never once uses it of an opportunity actually given after the end. Its root also supplies the ordinary Arabic word for blame between friends, the kind that expects to be answered and repaired.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repentance is presented as time bound, not as impossible. Nothing in the ayah says the door was shut against anyone; it says the hour for it has passed, which places the urgency in the reader's calendar rather than in God's willingness. The rest of the Quran is emphatic that the offer stands while life does. Setting the two statements together is what produces a working sense of a deadline, and this surah supplies the closing end of it.

crossReferences.why: Puts the other side of the same matter, telling those who went furthest not to despair of mercy.
Draws the same line in time, distinguishing repentance from what is offered only when death arrives.
Uses the identical closing verb, there after excuses are described as no longer useful.

studies.applyIt: Think of one apology you have been meaning to make and have kept postponing because the moment is never right. Not a large reckoning. One sentence to one person. Send it today, without a preamble explaining the delay. This ayah is about a window closing, and the most ordinary form of that is a conversation you keep intending to have.

studies.title: To Him Belongs The Greatness
studies.meaning: The surah ends by handing back the word it has spent thirty ayat taking away from people. Greatness belongs in the heavens and the earth to God, and the word used is the noun behind the accusation made earlier, that the objectors grew too great to listen. Before that comes a triple naming of lordship: of the heavens, of the earth, and of all peoples, so the praise is grounded in the two places the surah kept pointing at and then in the beings living there.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah opened by listing signs in the heavens, on the earth, in the alternation of night and day and in the human being's own making, and it repeatedly accused its audience of arrogance in the face of them. These two ayat close it. No occasion is reported. The commentators read the ending as deliberately answering the surah's own charge with the name that settles who greatness belongs to.

keyTerms.note: A noun for grandeur in its fullest sense, from the root behind arrogance. It occurs twice in the Quran: once on the lips of men refusing a prophet, who accused him of wanting it on earth, and once here.

The word is repeated three times in one line, attached to the heavens, then the earth, then all beings. Arabic could have joined them under a single mention, so the repetition is doing something: it separates the claims instead of bundling them.

From a root meaning to restrain or to set in order, the same root behind a bridle and behind a judgement. Wisdom in Arabic is less about knowing than about putting each thing exactly where it belongs.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Precedence was the currency of Meccan politics. Which clan held the keys of the sanctuary, who watered the pilgrims, whose word closed an argument in the assembly: these were the questions that occupied the city, and a man who could not claim greatness in some form had no place in the conversation. A closing line that removes greatness from the earth entirely was not abstract to that audience. It was an eviction.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for greatness used here occurs exactly twice in the Quran, and the two uses face each other. In the other place it is what Pharaoh's court accuses Moses and his brother of wanting on earth. The Book therefore puts the word once in a false claim and once in its only true home, and nowhere else at all.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Ending an argument with praise rather than with a verdict is a recurring move in the Quran, and it changes what the argument was for. The surah has been describing a court scene and a fire, and it finishes on a sentence that would be true if none of that had been mentioned. The two closing names hold the pair the whole chapter needed: power that cannot be resisted, and wisdom that places everything correctly, so the outcome described earlier is neither arbitrary nor merely strong.

crossReferences.why: Holds the only other use of the word for greatness, there as an accusation thrown at Moses.
Opens the Book with the same praise and the same title, Lord of all the worlds.
Lists the divine names in a similar closing sequence, ending on transcendence above all association.

studies.applyIt: Find one place today where you were going to claim something small: correcting a colleague on a detail nobody needs, adding the fact that you were right first, letting a compliment run. Let it pass without the addition. The surah spends its last line moving greatness off the earth, and the practice version of that is one sentence you decide not to say.
